title: A weekend in Jakarta — gue, lo and the -in verbs
goal: Understand the Indonesian of Jakarta's streets, trains and group chats, and use a little of it with friends without sounding like a textbook: *gue* and *lo*, verbs in *-in* and *nge-*, and the particles *kok, sih, deh, dong, kan* that carry the attitude.
bekal: recognise and use Jakarta pronouns *gue* and *lo*, and know when not to
turn *-kan* and *-i* verbs into Jakarta *-in* (*bantuin, beliin, doain*) and use *nge-* verbs (*ngemal, ngopi, nyari*)
hear the attitude in *kok, sih, deh, dong, kan, tuh* and answer in kind

notes: **Gue and lo** are Jakarta's "I" and "you", from the old Betawi dialect with a dash of Hokkien. Between friends in Jakarta they are warm and normal; with elders, bosses, strangers or in Yogyakarta they are rude or at least jarring. Sarah's instinct (*aku* with a friend) is the safe default anywhere in Indonesia.

**KRL** (said *ka-er-el*) is the electric commuter train that links Jakarta with Bogor, Depok, Tangerang and Bekasi. Manggarai is the big interchange, and at *jam pulang kantor* (going-home time) it is a test of character. Women-only carriages are at each end of the train.
**Ya iyalah** — "well, obviously", "duh". It answers a remark whose answer is self-evident, with a grin. It can sound dismissive if you are not friends; with Rina it is affection.

**Cie** (or *ciee*, drawn out) is the sound Indonesians make to tease someone about romance: when a colleague gets flowers, when a friend mentions a boyfriend's mother. *Calon* is "candidate, future": *calon suami* (fiancé), *calon mertua* (future parents-in-law).

**Apaan sih** — "what are you on about", "oh stop" — is the standard embarrassed deflection, usually with a smile that says the opposite. *Tau* at the end of a sentence (from *tahu*, know) means "you know", "just so you know".

**Dasar!** — literally "basis" — is short for *dasar kamu*, "that's so typical of you". It is exasperated but fond, like "honestly!" or "you're hopeless". *Ketularan* ("infected", from *tular*, to spread) is the adversative *ke-an* of Unit 11: something you caught without meaning to.

grammars.title: Pronouns in Jakarta
body: Indonesian lets you choose your "I" and "you" according to who you are talking to. In Jakarta, among friends and people your age, the choice is usually *gue* and *lo*.
after: The rule is symmetry: if someone uses *gue* with you, *lo* back is fine; if they use *saya* or *aku*, stay there. Using *gue* with Bu Endang would be like calling the Queen "mate".

⚠️ Mixing is normal and nobody minds: many Jakartans say *aku* to a partner and *gue* to friends, and Sarah's *aku* in a *gue* conversation is perfectly acceptable. The only real mistake is *lo* to someone older.
💬 *Gue* and *lo* also turn up in writing that wants to sound young: advertising, captions, comics. When you see them in a formal context, it is a deliberate choice of voice, not a mistake.

grammars.title: -in verbs and nge- verbs
body: Jakarta speech replaces both *-kan* and *-i* with a single ending, *-in*, and drops the formal *me-* in favour of the bare nasal or *nge-* (Unit 3).
after: *Nge-* can turn a noun into an activity: *ngemal* (mall), *ngopi* (coffee), *ngeteh* (tea), *ngegym* (gym), *nge-date*. It is productive, playful, and strictly spoken.
💬 *-in* is used across Indonesia by young people, not just in Jakarta, because of television and social media. In writing, even a text to your landlady, go back to *-kan* and *-i*.

notes: **Bule** is the everyday word for a white foreigner. It is mostly descriptive rather than hostile, and many *bule* in Indonesia use it about themselves with a shrug. Children in the provinces may shout *Bule!* in excitement; smiling and waving is the standard response.

**Ngaret** — to be late, from *karet* (rubber): time that stretches. *Jam karet* ("rubber time") is the national joke about punctuality, told by Indonesians about themselves. Mbak Nur would not find it funny.

**Ojol** is *ojek online*, the app-booked motorbike taxi, and a universal excuse. Likewise *gara-gara* ("because of", usually something annoying) is the spoken cousin of *karena*: *gara-gara hujan*, *gara-gara kamu*.

**Doang** is Jakarta's *saja* or *cuma*, but it comes after the word: *sekali doang* (just once), *lima ribu doang* (only five thousand). In the rest of the country people understand it and many use it.

**Pagian** — "a bit earlier". Casual Indonesian adds *-an* to adjectives and time words for "a bit more so": *pagian* (earlier), *gedean* (bigger), *pelanan* (slower), *cepetan!* (hurry up!). In writing you would say *lebih pagi*.

**Chat Indonesian.** *Wkwk* (or *wkwkwk*) is written laughter, *gaes* is "guys" spelled the way it sounds, *udah* and *temen* are the spoken forms of *sudah* and *teman*. Nobody uses capitals or full stops in a group chat; this book adds them so that you can read it.

grammars.title: Particles that carry the attitude
body: These little words have no dictionary meaning you can translate, but they change the whole tone of a sentence. Here is what each one adds, in the friendly register of this unit.

head: Particle
Adds
Example
Feel
rows: look at that / here you go

after: *Kok* has two faces: at the start of a question it is "how come?" (*Kok telat?*); at the end of a statement it reassures (*Nggak apa-apa, kok* — it's really fine). You have been hearing the second one since Unit 1.
⚠️ *Dong* with a request is only for friends (*Beliin, dong*). To anyone older or senior, it sounds like a demand; use *tolong* or *boleh minta …?* instead.

sections.title: Jakarta speech and its standard forms

blocks.text: Most "Jakarta" words are simply the standard word worn down by fast speech. Once you know the pairs, films, TikTok and your Jakarta friends become much easier to follow.

blocks.title: When to use Jakarta Indonesian
items: Yes: with friends your age in Jakarta, in group chats, when joking.
Carefully: with colleagues your own age, once they use it first.
No: with elders, officials, customers, teachers, your RT, or anyone in Central Java who has not used it with you.
A foreigner who can switch registers is admired; one who uses *gue* everywhere sounds as though they learned Indonesian from sitcoms.

blocks.text: Jakarta has more ways to get stuck than any city deserves, and more ways to get unstuck. These are the words for moving through it.
